offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years or such less punishment as is mentioned in the Act (for charge 1) and imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or such less punishment as is mentioned in the Act (for charges 4 and 5(c))
number_of_offences: 3 charges were charged and 3 charges were finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the first respondent made an observation about heart being an edible offal and reiterated it in his report, but noted that there was no evidence he instructed the butchery staff to accept heart as part of dressed meat.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that the Supervisory Officer and Veterinary Officer were charged and punished, indicating their credibility was not in question.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was dated 25.08.2000, the High Court decision was on 22.12.1995, and the Supreme Court decision was on 12.09.2011.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Y. Rajagopala Rao, R. Balasubramanyam, Y. Ramesh, Sureshta Bagga; Counsel for the State: P.P. Malhotra, ASG, Rajiv Nanda, Rahul Kaushik, B.K. Prasad (for B.V. Balaram Das)

appeal_history.trial_court: The High Court partially allowed the writ petition and quashed the order dated 22.12.1995.
appeal_history.high_court: The High Court's order was challenged in Crl. A. No. 876 of 2003, and the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order.
appeal_history.supreme_court: The Supreme Court allowed Criminal Appeal No. 876 of 2003 and set aside the High Court's order, and allowed Criminal Appeal No. 877 of 2003, setting aside the punishment of dismissal and substituting it with a lesser punishment.

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the High Court erred in quashing the order forfeiting the pension of the delinquent officer, asserting that the President of India has the power under Regulation 16(a) of the Pension Regulations to forfeit pension of an officer dismissed or cashiered by a General Court Martial, independent of the punishment imposed by the court martial.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court was correct in quashing the order forfeiting the pension, asserting that the punishment of dismissal was shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of the offences proved and that the findings of the General Court Martial were not perverse or irrational.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the power to deny pension as a consequence of an officer being cashiered or dismissed vests only with the President of India under Regulation 16(a) of the Pension Regulations, and that the punishment of dismissal is independent of the punishment imposed by the court martial.
precedent_relied_upon: Union of India v. P. D. Yadav 2001 (4) Suppl. SCR 209 = 2002 (1) sec 405; Brig. A. K. Malhotra v. Union of India (1997) (4) SLR 51; Union of India vs. Major A. Hussain 1997 (6) Suppl. SCR 218 = 1998 (1) sec 537; Ranjit Thakur vs. Union of India 1988 (1) SeR 512 = 1987 (4) sec 611; Union of India vs. R.K. Sharma 2001 (9) Sec 492
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the punishment of dismissal from service was found to be shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of the offences proved, and the court substituted it with a lesser punishment of forfeiture of eight years of service for the purpose of pension and a severe reprimand.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered that the charges were technical in nature, the role of the Commandant was limited, and the omissions attributed to the respondent were actually omissions by his subordinates.
other_sentence_order: The court directed the authorities to process and settle the pension claim of the respondent, and the respondent will not be entitled to any back-wages from the date of his dismissal to the date of his superannuation.
